Hence, total valid min-heaps $= 20 \times 2 \times 2 = 80$.

questions.explaination: A binary heap storing $n$ keys is an almost complete binary tree whose height in terms of edges is $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$. For $n = 32$, the height is $\lfloor \log_2 32 \rfloor = 5$.
questions.question_text_latex: The height of any rooted tree is defined as the maximum number of edges in the path from the root node to any leaf node. Suppose a Min-Heap $T$ stores 32 keys. The height of $T$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\. (Answer in integer)

questions.explaination:
The function `foo` counts 1 whenever two consecutive adjacent elements differ ($S[0] 
eq S[1]$), plus 1 for the base case `size == 1`. In array $A = \{0, 1, 2, 2, 2, 0, 0, 1, 1\}$, adjacent transitions where $A[i] 
eq A[i+1]$ occur at indices: $0 	o 1$ ($0 
eq 1$), $1 	o 2$ ($1 
eq 2$), $4 	o 5$ ($2 
eq 0$), and $6 	o 7$ ($0 
eq 1$). There are 4 such differences, plus 1 returned at `size == 1`, giving $4 + 1 = 5$.

The loop inspects each node following the head of `L1` (`ptr1->next`). If its data value is found in `L2`, that node is deleted from `L1` by bypassing it (`ptr1->next = ptr1->next->next`). Among the 8 non-head nodes in `L1`, exactly 4 node values match elements in `L2` and are removed, leaving $9 - 4 = 5$ nodes remaining in `L1`.

For $n = 14362$, the first loop computes $t = 10000$. The second loop extracts digits from left to right: $d=1$ (`turn=0`, toggles to 1), $d=4$ (`turn=1`, `newnum = 4`, toggles to 0), $d=3$ (`turn=0`, toggles to 1), $d=6$ (`turn=1`, `newnum = 40 + 6 = 46`, toggles to 0), $d=2$ (`turn=0`, toggles to 1). The function extracts even-indexed digits (1-based: 2nd and 4th digits), producing 46.

questions.question_text:
Consider a binary tree 𝑇 in which every node has either zero or two children.
Let 𝑛> 0 be the number of nodes in 𝑇.
Which ONE of the following is the number of nodes in 𝑇 that have exactly two
children?

options.D:
𝑛+ 1
2

Organising Institute: IIT Roorkee

questions.explaination: In any proper (strictly) binary tree with $L$ leaves and $I$ internal nodes (nodes with 2 children), $L = I + 1$. Since $n = L + I = 2I + 1$, the number of internal nodes is $I = \frac{n-1}{2}$.
questions.question_text_latex: Consider a binary tree $T$ in which every node has either zero or two children. Let $n > 0$ be the number of nodes in $T$. Which ONE of the following is the number of nodes in $T$ that have exactly two children?

options.D:
Hello World!d!

Organising Institute: IIT Roorkee

questions.subtopic: Programming in C: pointers and strings
questions.explaination: `stringcopy(a, a + 2)` copies string `"Hello World!"` into the start of array `a`, overwriting the first 12 characters. The copy stops when `*t` hits null terminator without copying the null terminator over `d!`, leaving trailing `d!\0`, resulting in `"Hello World!d!"`.

questions.subtopic: Programming in C: loops and Euclidean GCD
questions.explaination: The do-while loop implements the subtraction-based Euclidean algorithm for greatest common divisor: $\gcd(x, y) = \gcd(126, 105) = 21$.

questions.question_text:
Suppose the values 10, −4, 15, 30, 20, 5, 60, 19 are inserted in that order into an
initially empty binary search tree. Let 𝑇 be the resulting binary search tree.
The number of edges in the path from the node containing 19 to the root node of 𝑇
is ___________. (Answer in integer)

Organising Institute: IIT Roorkee
questions.explaination: Insert keys into BST: 10 is root $\to$ 15 goes right $\to$ 30 goes right $\to$ 20 goes left $\to$ 19 goes left of 20. The path from root is $10 \to 15 \to 30 \to 20 \to 19$, which contains 4 edges.
questions.question_text_latex: Suppose the values 10, $-4$, 15, 30, 20, 5, 60, 19 are inserted in that order into an initially empty binary search tree. Let $T$ be the resulting binary search tree. The number of edges in the path from the node containing 19 to the root node of $T$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_. (Answer in integer)

questions.question_text:
A meld operation on two instances of a data structure combines them into one single
instance of the same data structure. Consider the following data structures:
P: Unsorted doubly linked list with pointers to the head node and tail node
of the list.
Q: Min-heap implemented using an array.
R: Binary Search Tree.
Which ONE of the following options gives the worst-case time complexities for
meld operation on instances of size 𝑛 of these data structures?

options.A: P: Θ(1), Q: Θ(𝑛), R: Θ(𝑛)
options.B: P: Θ(1), Q: Θ(𝑛log 𝑛), R: Θ(𝑛)
options.C: P: Θ(𝑛), Q: Θ(𝑛log 𝑛), R: Θ(𝑛2)
options.D:
P: Θ(1), Q: Θ(𝑛), R: Θ(𝑛log 𝑛)

Organising Institute: IIT Roorkee

questions.subtopic: Data structures: heaps, linked lists and merge operations
questions.explaination: Merging two circular linked lists takes $\Theta(1)$ by swapping pointers. Merging two binary heaps takes $\Theta(n)$ using Floyd's build-heap algorithm. Hence, time complexities are $P: \Theta(1), Q: \Theta(n), R: \Theta(n)$.
questions.question_text_latex: A meld operation on two instances of a data structure combines them into one single instance of the same data structure. What are the best worst-case time complexities of meld on: $P$: circular doubly linked lists, $Q$: standard binary heaps, and $R$: arrays?

questions.question_text:
Consider a stack data structure into which we can PUSH and POP records. Assume
that each record pushed in the stack has a positive integer key and that all keys are
distinct.
We wish to augment the stack data structure with an 𝑂(1) time MIN operation that
returns a pointer to the record with smallest key present in the stack
1) without deleting the corresponding record, and
2) without increasing the complexities of the standard stack operations.
Which one or more of the following approach(es) can achieve it?

options.A:
Keep with every record in the stack, a pointer to the record with the smallest key
below it.
options.B: Keep a pointer to the record with the smallest key in the stack.
options.C:
Keep an auxiliary array in which the key values of the records in the stack are
maintained in sorted order.
options.D:
Keep a Min-Heap in which the key values of the records in the stack are maintained.

Organising Institute: IIT Roorkee

questions.explaination: To retrieve the minimum key in $O(1)$ while maintaining $O(1)$ push and pop, each record (or stack node) can store a pointer to the record containing the minimum key at or below that stack level.
questions.question_text_latex: Consider a stack data structure into which we can PUSH and POP records. Assume that each record has a numeric key. Which of the following strategies allows finding the record with the minimum key in $O(1)$ worst-case time without increasing the asymptotic time for PUSH and POP?

options_latex.A: Keep with every record in the stack, a pointer to the record with the smallest key below it.
options_latex.B: Keep a pointer to the record with the smallest key in the stack.
options_latex.C: Keep an auxiliary array in which the key values of the records in the stack are maintained in sorted order.
options_latex.D: Keep a Min-Heap in which the key values of the records in the stack are maintained.
